Abstract
Despite the European Union's strong commitment to transparent and participatory governance, the preparation of its position for international climate negotiations is

The situation could be said to reflect a broader paradigm of secrecy in EU policy- and law-making. This paper discusses factors that uphold the secrecy in the EU preparation for climate negotiations and how that secrecy could dispelled to some extent. In addition, the analysis provides recommendations for how better civil society participation could be achieved without putting the confidentiality of the international climate negotiations or the EU's strategic ends at risk.
1 | INTRODUCTION

The EU's mandate to act in the international legal order stems from its international legal personality as established in the Treaty on

European Union (TEU)1 and recognised by the members, institutions, and instruments of the international system. In international climate negotiations, the EU “speaks with one voice” - representing 27 sovereign Member States. Forging a common negotiation position is a lengthy and complicated process, one involv-
ing an array of institutions and actors, many phases, and serious inter-

For citizens and stakeholders, the process through which the EU arrives at its common position for international climate negotiations may seem rather opaque and arcane. Indeed, it is far from common knowledge how the EU formulates its position and, even more saliently, how relevant information can be accessed and what oppor-

Then again, an open and participatory policy-making process requires additional time and resources on the part of the policymaker, with no guarantee that these will bring added value.

Against this background, and bearing in mind the EU's strong commitment to transparent and participatory governance, this paper examines the transparency and openness of the Union's preparation for the United Nations (UN) climate negotiations. The paper asks whether civil society can access information on the relevant policy-
makers and documents, whether there are opportunities for civil soci-

ety organisations (CSOs) to participate in the preparatory process, and to what extent the EU position is available for public scrutiny before the negotiation sessions. The discussion also reflects upon the pre-

2 | TRANSPARENCY AND PUBLIC PARTICIPATION AS FOUNDATIONAL ELEMENTS OF EU CLIMATE POLICYMAKING

The term ‘transparency’ does not have a clear-cut definition15 In broad terms, transparency could be characterised as a ‘culture or scheme in which relevant information (on law and politics) is avail-

able.’16 In strict terms, transparency is distinguished from openness in that it may only mean making documents available to the public, whereas openness also encompasses participation.17 However, in the

EU, the two terms are arguably close to being synonymous.18 In any case, transparency is critical for effective public participation19 in ensuring access to information an essential prerequisite for and first step toward effective public participation. The accessible information may be related to the substance of public policymaking or concern the procedures and objectives driving such activity. Significantly, transparency does not only encompass the passive right of actors to access information; the concept subsumes the broader and more pro-
active duty of government to ensure that substantive and procedural information is provided in an accessible fashion.20
Transparency is often seen as contributing to improved informa-
tion and knowledge, legitimacy and accountability, participatory
democracy and good governance, and the rule of law.21 Yet, from pol-
icymakers' perspective, efforts to ensure transparency and enable par-
ticipation usually entail extra costs and require time. This may detract from policymakers interest in providing such opportunities.22
Transparency, openness, and public participation are all core values of good governance.23 Indeed all are enshrined in the founding

The TFEU contains provisions that apply to situations in which the EU is engaged in international environmental negotiations.

According to Article 218, it is the Council that authorises the opening of negotiations, adopts negotiating directives, authorises the signing of agreements, and concludes them. The Commission (with the team that it has built) is the actual negotiator. An exception to the provi-

3.2.1 | The Council: the leader

The Council of the EU leads the process where the EU position is shaped and agreed on in anticipation of the UN climate negotiations and, in particular, the COPs. The Council is an institution under which government ministers from each Member State meet to discuss, amend, and adopt EU legislation and coordinate EU policies. The pol-
icy area under discussion determines the composition of the Council;
for climate policy, it is usually the environmental and/or climate minis-
ters who make decisions (forming the Environment Council). The pres-

Council is a key decision-making body in the EU, and part of its man-

(consensus).48
The final products of the preparatory process for UN climate negotiations are a document known as the Council Conclusions, a negotiation mandate, and the accompanying negotiating directives.
The Conclusions, adopted typically one to two months in advance of a
UN climate conference, outline the EU position in the negotiations.

The content of the Conclusions, a document typically 10 to 20 pages in length, is legally non-binding and relatively general in nature,49 highlighting the EU's climate action and commitment, urging other parties to act, and outlining the EU's general priorities for the negotiations.

The EU certainly sees no reason why it should do so,133 and European civil society surely understands this as well.

The dilemma is that, on the one hand, a lack of transparency may have serious impacts on the public legitimacy of the outcome of the process. Enhanced transparency would strengthen the Council's accountability and enable public pressure on those Member States standing in the way of a compromise or blocking a more ambitious position. On the other hand, one could argue that finding a common position within the Council could become even more difficult if the deliberations, including individual Member States' positions and argu-

The Council is the most important EU institution in the prepara-

6 | ‘CRACKS’ IN THE SECRECY PARADIGM: TOWARD MORE EFFECTIVE PARTICIPATION
6.1 | Necessary confidentiality or excessive secrecy?

Confidentiality is necessary to secure effective negotiations. The point where necessary confidentiality becomes excessive secrecy is difficult to determine, especially by actors who approach the process from dif-
ferent positions. Yet, the fact is that the EU is today quite unique among the UNFCCC parties in the degree of openness it affords citi-
zens regarding its position ahead of negotiations.
Regulation 1049/2001 on Access to Documents is often referred to as the legal basis for making EU documents public. However, the
Regulation is not readily applicable to transparency in the case of doc-
uments that relate to the EU's international negotiations. Article 4(1)
(a) of the Regulation provides an exception to the publicity of the doc-

uments held by the European Parliament, Council, and Commission in cases where access might undermine the protection of the public interest as regards international relations. This exception has since been assessed and elaborated by the CJEU138 and the European
Ombudsman139 in the specific context of international treaty negotia-
tions in which the EU is engaged.
In practice, the EU institutions have wide discretion under Regu-

7 | CONCLUSION

Even though the EU comprises 27 sovereign Member States, it speaks with one voice in the UN climate negotiations. This is a result of a long preparatory process that involves a range of institutions and actors, many phases, and serious internal negotiation and coordination.

Although the EU is committed to promoting transparency, openness, and public participation in its decision-making – the values of good governance that are enshrined in the founding treaties – the prepara-

tion of the Union's position for international climate negotiations is not particularly transparent or open to civil society participation. This observation follows the line of criticism that is frequently presented of the preparation of EU legislation, one singling out the Council as disappointingly secretive in its decision-making. The study has found that the criticism of the transparency and openness of the preparation of EU legislation partly applies to the process through which the EU prepares its position for international climate negotiations. The relevant meetings of the Council and prepa-
ratory bodies are not open to the public. Neither the Member States'

positions and arguments presented in the preparatory meetings nor the technical background papers and briefings made available to the preparatory meetings are public. While the meeting agendas of the Council's preparatory bodies are generally available, the composi-

CSOs can make their views known in the process through occasional expert presentations and informal communication with Member

CSOs' efforts to engage in the EU preparation for the climate negotiations.
The degree of confidentiality, or secrecy, as regards the prepara-
tion of the EU position for the UN climate negotiations is significant.
No direct comparison can be drawn with the preparation of the EU's domestic legislation. The setting for the former – international negotiation – places inherent limitations on transparency and open-
ness, given the shared negotiation competence between the EU and the Member States and the non-legally binding outcome of the nego-

tiations. Moreover, the EU has, in Article 4 of Regulation 1049/2001 on Access to Documents, a legally valid basis for preventing public access to the preparatory documents if publicity would undermine the interests of the EU in international relations.

The concerns voiced about the internal secrecy paradigm seem to apply to some extent to the EU's preparation for the international climate negotiations. However, to best capture the views of the EU officials interviewed for this study, one could ask the following ques-

tion: Given that the EU already is the UNFCCC party that is by far the most open about its position in the negotiations, could the Union's preparatory process be any more open without seriously jeopardising its interests in the negotiations? This research asserts that the EU need not markedly increase the openness of the preparatory process, whereas civil society could use the existing degree of openness more effectively.
